Indicators and classiﬁcation of food security status
The level at which food security is of interest, i.e., household, community, district, or country, determines which factors should be
assessed.
International food security phase classiﬁcation (IPC) for countries
For example, the IPC provides guidance to countries for classifying a country’s regions and subregions. It emphasizes that as much as
possible existing and relevant information should be used, and that there is no ﬁxed set of indicators and methods to refer to.
Table 1 shows the ﬁve stages of food security that are distinguished in this IPC classiﬁcation together with proposed indicators
and their cut-offs for the different stages. Some indicators reﬂect context and livelihood assets, such as civil security, “structural”
(underlying hindrances to food security), livelihood assets/capital; some reﬂect vulnerability, such as hazards, destitution/displace-
ment; others reﬂect underlying causes of malnutrition such as water access/availability, food access/availability, dietary diversity; the
top ones reﬂect outcome, i.e., crude mortality rate (/10,000 day1), disease, acute malnutrition (wasting), and stunting. Some of
